conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling very nauseous and vomiting since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up feeling awful. I’ve thrown up greenish fluid several times. I tried to take my pills but I just vomited them right back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you’ve had this happen before—about 10 times in the last three months?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But after my last hospital stay, my GI doctor adjusted my gastric pacer and gave me new meds. I was fine for a full week—then this hit again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. Your vitals show high blood pressure and a fast heart rate, which we often see during these episodes. We’ll start IV fluids and give you some anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be enough? Last time, nothing helped until they adjusted the pacer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran, Reglan, and Compazine now. But we’ll also check if there’s another issue. An abdominal X-ray was done—no blockage, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My blood sugar was high earlier—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick glucose was 349. Since you’re not eating, we’ve started a lower dose of Lantus insulin and will use Humalog as needed. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night were stable—no infection in blood cultures, kidney function is normal. But your heart rate is still in the 110s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel anxious, but I know it’s from being so sick. Is the fast heart rate dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a stress response to nausea and vomiting. It usually improves when symptoms do. We’re watching it on telemetry, and your ECG shows just sinus tachycardia—no heart damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering an endoscopy. Since you’ve had esophagitis before, we want to check if that’s flaring up or if the pylorus is too tight, slowing stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that last time. They found esophagitis and adjusted my pacer. Could we do something more this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If the pylorus is tight, we can inject Botox to relax it. It’s been helpful for some patients with gastroparesis like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds worth trying. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled it for tomorrow morning. For now, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and continue the anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is still high—188/88. We gave hydralazine yesterday, but it’s not fully controlled. We’ll restart your lisinopril once you can keep pills down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on lisinopril for years. Should I be concerned it’s not working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely because you haven’t been able to take it. Once we restart it and your nausea improves, we expect your BP to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Any update on the endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still on for today. We’ll also repeat your chest X-ray to check your port and lungs. You had a portable one last night—heart size is normal, lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you for your endoscopy. You’ll be sedated, and the GI team will look at your esophagus and stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And they’ll do the Botox if needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if they see the pylorus is tight. We’ll update you when you wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy went well. You had some inflammation and a small ulcer at the bottom of your esophagus—consistent with reflux. The stomach was empty, which confirms delayed emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Botox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they injected Botox into the pylorus to help it relax. This should help food move from your stomach into the intestine more easily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Do I need to stay on the same meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on Protonix twice daily for the esophagitis, and continue Reglan and erythromycin to help stomach motility. Your nausea should start improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you made it through the night without vomiting. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually feeling less nauseous. Could the Botox be working already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. It can take a few days, but some patients feel better quickly. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart rate is still high—118. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still elevated, but it’s coming down slowly. As your nausea improves, we expect your heart rate and blood pressure to normalize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated clear liquids well. We’re going to try a soft diabetic diet—mashed potatoes, applesauce, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry for real food. Can I have insulin with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart your full insulin regimen—Lantus at night and Humalog before meals. Your glucose was 153 this morning—well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any other labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low yesterday—2.9—so we gave supplements. This morning it’s 3.4, which is better but still a bit low. We’ll keep giving potassium with your meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize that could happen. Is it from vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Losing fluids through vomiting can deplete potassium. We’re replacing it, so it should normalize soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two meals and no vomiting. Your heart rate is down to 98, and BP is 138/82. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Are my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—same doses. Continue Protonix twice daily, Reglan four times a day, erythromycin three times a day, and your insulin. Use Zofran or the suppository if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor in one week to check how you’re doing with the Botox. Also follow up with your endocrinologist for diabetes management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you can’t keep food or liquids down, or if you have chest pain, high fever, or vomit blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for getting me through this episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. The Botox may help reduce how often this happens. We’ll keep working to get you more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really hope so. Ten admissions in three months is too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re all on your side. Let’s aim for fewer trips back. Your husband can pick you up around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: He’ll be relieved. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed, but I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in—how are you feeling after breakfast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still no nausea. I ate most of my oatmeal and drank tea. I think I’m really turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so grateful. This episode was scary, but I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Keep up with your diet, meds, and follow-up. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will come by to review your medications and discharge instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve got my list. I’ll take everything as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge labs show mild anemia and low potassium, but both are improving. No need for transfusion or extra treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I take iron or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless your outpatient doctor recommends it. Focus on nutrition and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you for everything.
